title: MZ Need to Fit Menus and Other UI Within Lower Resolution

posts.author: ImpSassy
posts.body:
Please have mercy on me. I do not understand forums. I never have. I'm trying my best to put this where I feel it most belongs, so if I'm wrong I ask you assist me in migrating the post rather than just deleting it.
With that being said, hello! I'm currently working on a project that aims to recapture the vibes of the CGB-001, a.k.a. the Nintendo GameBoy Colour. I was primarily inspired by Lufia: The Legend Returns, which despite being a rather mundane release with questionable localisation, is hands down one of the most vibrant and detailed games on the platform, at least that was released within its proper lifespan. Disclosed is what the current version looks like. GB Studio was used to ensure the palettes chosen were as accurate as possible to the GBC's limited 15-Bit colour gamut. It's running at native 160x144 resolution, upscaled by 4x. Plugins were used to sharpen the image and remove the Touch Menu button.
Overall I am supremely happy with how it's turning out visually, but I'm running into a major hiccup with the UI. Pardon the silly title screen placeholder image.
As you can see, the in-game UI is completely broken from the lower resolution. I did attempt to scale down the UI manually to match the game's base resolution, but the results are even more busted, I imagine due to the fact the engine has no built-in scaling system for the UI. Also keep in mind I also simplified the UI when I scaled it down, but rest assured using the standard, full-colour version scaled down results in the same errors, including the blackened text.
So I am looking for
any
guidance here. Whether it's "use MV instead" or "use such-and-such plugin" or what have you. The only thing I don't want to hear is "Oh, why not just fully commit to GB Studio instead of trying to brute force the project into MZ?" because I simply feel I have much more freedom with RPG Maker's framework than I would with GB Studio.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
It's a common question that comes up. Coincidentally, not long after your own post another user had the exact same question.
This really is a matter of fixed pixel values.
Ui elements have fixed values, such as icon sizes and padding. Shrinking the resolution down too much is going to butt into these limitations.
It is better to, instead of scaling the resolution down, scale the assets up.
So instead of 160x144, you might consider 320x288
(which is likely still too small) and scale your assets up by 2x
Regardless, the engine is not designed to do small sizes like this, it was not built to make Gameboy games, so in order to work to convey that same "small size" you're going to have to find often times complicated or tedious solutions.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
I personally have not looked into any small resolution plugin options - they may be available considering the frequency at which it is requested.
Even still, it would not be a one-size-fits-all scenario. While the plugin may be able to handle all of the default UI that RM comes with OTB, it would not account for any additional UI generated by other plugins. Depending on what you are designing, this could be a limiting factor.
Considering your post implies utilizing other engines, even within the RM releases, you might consider trying much older versions such as 2000/2003 or XP which were built at a time where much smaller resolutions like that were practical.
While official support for those engines ended long ago, there are still a handful of community members here who swear by those engines and may be able to provide additional support.
What I personally recommend is make a couple of small games. Set yourself a rigid time frame to stick to, such as 1 week, and make a short game within that time span. The goal is not to make something fun, but instead to learn how the engine works and if it suits your needs.
Use this strategy to demo alternate engines and see if any of them come closer to your needs.
(broadly speaking, we also tend to recommend users make small games first before pursuing their dream game anyway, so by it's very nature, doing this demo is also fulfilling that 'learn the thing before doing the dream game' thing.)

posts.author: Kenen
posts.body: The entirety of the UI is hard coded in fixed dimensions. If you’re interested in a pixel-perfect 1px presentation for whatever reason, you’re better off creating a perfect 3x version and scaling the game window down via a plugin.
